title: Annotating Implicit Reasoning in Arguments with Causal Links
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to represent implicit reasoning in arguments in a way that makes the connection between a claim and its supporting premise more explicit. The authors argue that existing approaches to implicit knowledge in arguments often capture either commonsense facts or free-text explanations, but do not reliably explain the causal reasoning that links argumentative components.

To address this, they propose a semi-structured annotation scheme based on causal links, inspired by the Argument from Consequences scheme. The scheme breaks an argument into an action entity, an outcome entity, and implicit causal knowledge, connected by cause or suppress relations. The paper also introduces a two-phase crowdsourcing workflow for generating and then filtering these annotations: Phase 1 collects candidate implicit reasonings from crowdworkers, and Phase 2 filters them using additional crowd judgments about validity and quality.

The empirical setting is a corpus of English-language political and social debate arguments drawn from the IBM-Rank-30K dataset, with arguments filtered to six debatable topics and support-stance claims only. The work is not an educational intervention study; it is a natural language processing / argument mining annotation study. The main conclusion is that the proposed scheme can achieve broad coverage, but quality is mixed: many annotations survive majority-vote filtering, yet expert review suggests that less than half of sampled annotations are high quality, indicating that the crowdsourcing process and filtering strategy need improvement.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a methodology/annotation paper about crowdsourcing semi-structured implicit reasoning in arguments, not an evaluation of an educational intervention or student outcome. It reports inter-annotator agreement and dataset statistics rather than a causal study in K-12 education.
impact_tier_rationale: No learner-facing intervention, academic outcome, or K-12 impact is evaluated. The paper’s contribution is infrastructural/natural language processing oriented, so there is no evidence of educational effect to score.
